analysis:
The PR changes only docs/architecture/inference.md (head lines 1030-1048). It adds a description of a PromptTokenCache in LocalTokenizerBridge, along with ChatTemplateLoopRewrites. No executable code is supplied, so this pass cannot verify the implementation and no source-level regression can be established.

Security-relevant claims in the documentation:
- Token-ID reuse is keyed to the same prefix-cache scope, and the doc says reuse never crosses a cache scope. This is consistent with the coordinator-authored cacheScope in T-041(d). If the implementation instead keyed on a global or caller-controlled scope, it would add a cross-account timing or sharing channel. That would be a new TTFT-like oracle, because a cached encode is faster than an uncached one. It would also be a plaintext-derived in-memory cache of prompt pieces (A-001) that T-041 does not currently cover.
- The doc says the cache is off without a scope, which matches the existing coordinator text-prefix-reuse posture. It does not state this for the new cache, so it is unverified.
- Linear-time rewrites of the Gemma 4 and GPT-OSS chat templates are said to render identically to the served template. The doc says sampled background comparisons disable reuse on mismatch. A rewrite that diverges from the served template could change the prompt the model sees, affecting output integrity and tool or role-injection handling. The doc describes fallback mitigations, but they are unverified.
- Four-core parallel encoding of long prompts is a modest CPU cost that may interact with availability (T-010, T-029). Nothing is bounded in the doc.
- The kill switch DARKBLOOM_TTFT_PROMPT_CACHE=0 is documented.

Open questions for deeper review of the code in PromptTokenCache.swift: the cache scope derivation, memory bounds and eviction, whether prompt text or tokens are retained after a scope ends or on unload, and whether T-041 needs an addendum covering the prompt-token cache as a timing channel. The doc-only evidence supports no concrete finding.
